source.title: SASSHA: Sharpness-aware Adaptive Second-order Optimization with Stable Hessian Approximation
source.authors: Dahun Shin; Dongyeop Lee; J. Chung; Namhoon Lee

record.tranche_reason: The study measures several sharpness metrics and validation performance across optimizers, testing whether sharpness relates to generalization with methods different from the magnitude-aware measure in V7.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports sharpness metrics and validation loss/accuracy for five optimizers. These measurements do not test the magnitude-aware perturbation measure specified in V7, so the rows are mapped to none. Other optimizer comparisons and ablations are not extracted unless they report sharpness or validation performance bearing on the claim.
record.test_reason: The study bears on V4 through its own comparisons of SGD with AdamW and adaptive second-order optimizers across image-classification settings, including broader hyperparameter tuning. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors associate existing approximate second-order optimizers with sharper solutions and poorer validation performance, and propose SASSHA to reduce sharpness while stabilizing Hessian estimates. They report improved performance, efficient lazy Hessian updates, and label-noise robustness; they do not establish that sharpness causally explains generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares optimizers and conventional sharpness measurements; it does not reproduce the magnitude-aware sharpness procedure described in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture vary in Appendix A; the main Table 1 comparison is ResNet-32 on CIFAR-100.

fits_no_version.finding: Conventional Hessian and fixed-radius loss-perturbation measures accompany optimizer differences in validation performance; these are not magnitude-aware measures or explicit generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conventional sharpness measures can correlate with validation performance across optimizer solutions, with the relationship depending on workload and measure.

fits_no_version.finding: SASSHA improves validation performance through a deliberately sharpness-minimizing optimization recipe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stable Hessian preconditioning combined with sharpness minimization can improve optimizer performance on the evaluated workloads.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The main sharpness comparison is one model and dataset; it reports validation rather than test accuracy or an explicit train-test error gap. The supplied Table 1 text is flattened for validation-loss values, preventing secure row assignment. The paper describes correlations but does not test the magnitude-aware measure in V7.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A Table 7 reports additional sharpness and validation measurements across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Wikitext-2 settings. These are left out to prioritize Table 1 results within the 60-row limit; they use conventional rather than magnitude-aware sharpness measures and therefore do not map to V7.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels paired with natural-label and random-label held-out performance. Partial label corruption experiments do not establish this.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

The restriction to tuning only learning rates and schedules; matched training performance; switching Adam to SGD; controlled isolation of decoupled weight decay. Language experiments have no SGD comparator.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Controlled dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, training-to-test error gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing high-memorization examples and retraining against random-removal controls.

missing.what: SGD versus AdamW validation accuracies across all six image workloads, including AdamW's ViT advantage and ResNet-20 tie. Record the learning-rate, weight-decay, and schedule search conditions.
Adaptive second-order versus SGD image comparisons beyond the extracted ResNet-32/CIFAR-100 setting, including ViT/AdaHessian 66.42±0.23 versus SGD 62.90±0.36%.
SGD versus AdamW with doubled epoch budgets: AdamW remains below SGD on the five convolutional workloads but exceeds it on ViT (66.97 versus 63.64%).

Adaptive second-order versus SGD validation accuracy under 20%, 40%, and 60% label corruption, where several disadvantages shrink or reverse; for example CIFAR-100 at 40% noise gives AdaHessian 58.37±0.13 versus SGD 55.78±0.55%.
missing.locator: Section 6.1, Table 5; Appendix L, Table 21; Appendix E.3

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly treats every version as untested: optimizer comparisons bear on V4, including its broader-tuning qualification. Broad tuning means these experiments cannot directly establish the limited-tuning clause. Table 1's flattened extraction shifts multiple sharpness values into the wrong columns; Table 7 helps resolve the assignments. No V7 verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD generalization under the stated tuning regimes.
Dropout effects across training-set sizes and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples.

relationships.condition: ResNet-32/CIFAR-100, adaptive second-order optimizers with broader tuning
relationships.reason: R22–R24 and R26–R29 show higher validation loss and lower accuracy for AdaHessian, Sophia-H, and Shampoo than SGD, even with weight-decay and method-specific tuning.
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdaHessian, Sophia-H, and Shampoo results have higher validation loss and lower accuracy than SGD, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: AdamW versus SGD on CIFAR-10/ResNet-32, CIFAR-100/ResNet-32 and WRN-28-10, and ImageNet/ResNet-50
relationships.reason: Missing Table 2 rows show AdamW below SGD: 92.42 versus 92.69, 68.78 versus 69.32, 79.09 versus 80.06, and 75.38 versus 75.58% despite broader tuning; verdict rests on text.
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdamW accuracy trails SGD across the specified CIFAR and ImageNet settings despite broader tuning, but the comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: AdamW versus SGD on CIFAR-10/ResNet-20 and ImageNet/ViT-s-32
relationships.reason: Missing Table 2 rows show effectively equal accuracy on ResNet-20 (92.04 versus 92.03%) and an AdamW advantage on ViT (66.46 versus 62.90%), consistent with V4's qualified scope; verdict rests on text.
relationships.display_finding: AdamW reportedly matched SGD accuracy on ResNet-20 and exceeded it on ViT-s-32, but both comparisons remain unverified.
